issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Asha had been at a crowded civic rally outside city hall when the man-made disaster occurred, and the memory of it still arrived in fragments that felt more like flashes than a story she could tell in order. She remembered the sudden crush of bodies, the sharp metallic smell in the air, shouting that turned panicked almost instantly, and the jolt of realizing there was no clear, safe direction to move. As a City Council Member, she had been expected to stay visible and composed, but in the weeks afterward that sense of public responsibility became tangled with fear. She began to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. The belief did not stay abstract; it settled into her body and decisions. Asha found herself on guard all the time, scanning crowds, watching people’s hands and faces, and feeling that she had to identify escape routes before she could feel comfortable anywhere.

Her sense of threat was strongest at night. Even in her apartment, she would pause by the door, note the window latches, and look down the hallway before she allowed herself to relax, though she rarely did. Unfamiliar places were worse. When council work required her to attend community meetings in neighborhoods she did not know well, she would refuse if she could, saying she needed the details in advance, though what she meant was that she could not assess the danger. If she could not map a room or a route out of it, she felt exposed and trapped in the same way she had felt during the disaster. That sense of threat fed a darker conclusion: if danger could appear anywhere and at any moment, then the world really was unsafe, and she could not afford to let her guard down even briefly.

Those appraisals shaped her days. Asha avoided physical stress because she had come to associate a racing heart, shortness of breath, or feeling physically taxed with being vulnerable and unable to respond quickly if something happened. She declined long walks between sites, took elevators instead of stairs when she could, and arranged her schedule to minimize anything that left her feeling depleted. She also became relentless in the small rituals of protection that organized her movements through the city. At work she sat where she could see entrances, kept her back away from open spaces, and constantly scanned the environment for signs of threat. In meetings she watched for the kind of person who might become dangerous, her attention drifting from the agenda to exits, doorways, and anyone moving too quickly.

Over time, those habits narrowed her life and made the world feel even more threatening. Because she was always checking, always braced, she noticed every unfamiliar sound, every raised voice, every unexpected movement, and each one seemed to confirm that her caution was necessary. The more she avoided unfamiliar places and physical strain, the less she felt she could tolerate them, and the less she trusted herself to manage if something went wrong. She found herself sitting through council sessions with her shoulders rigid, calculating the quickest way out before she could focus on the discussion. At night, the apartment felt less like a refuge than a place where she had to remain alert to prove she was safe. She slept lightly, waking at the slightest noise, and would lie in the dark thinking that she could not afford to miss anything. The pattern made her increasingly isolated; she stopped accepting invitations after hours, and friends noticed she was always the first to leave.

By the time she sought help, Asha was exhausted by the effort of staying safe. She had continued to function publicly, but only by living in a state of constant watchfulness that left her drained and increasingly cut off from the parts of the city and her job that once mattered to her. What brought her in was the fear that the vigilance itself was taking over her life, yet she remained most afraid that if she stopped scanning, stopped planning every exit, or walked into the wrong place unprepared, something terrible would happen and she would not be able to protect herself.
